opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the ultimate promise of mechanistic interpretability is that it could let us stop treating these systems as black boxes, and stop judging them only by their outputs.

Right now, when we evaluate an AI system, we mostly look at its behavior. We give it tests, red-team it, and see what it does. The problem is that behavior can come apart from what's actually going on inside. A system could behave well during training and evaluation because it has genuinely good goals. Or it could behave well because it has learned that behaving well is what gets rewarded, while having different underlying goals. Or it could be somewhere in between, with a messy mix of drives it doesn't fully understand itself. From the outside, those cases can look identical, at least until the stakes get high enough that they don't.

So the dream of interpretability is something like a mind-reading tool. You'd look at the internal computations and say: here's what it's actually representing, here's what it's actually optimizing for, here's whether it believes what it's telling us. If we had that, we could catch deception directly instead of hoping it shows up in behavior. We could check whether alignment techniques actually worked, rather than just whether they produced nice-looking outputs. And it would give us a much better feedback loop for alignment research generally, because right now we're partly flying blind.

That said, I want to be honest about my uncertainty about how fast it will get there. The field has made real progress: finding features, tracing circuits, understanding pieces of how models do certain tasks. But there's a big gap between understanding some circuits in a model and being able to confidently audit a frontier system's goals. My worry is that capabilities are advancing quickly, and we might reach very powerful systems before interpretability is mature enough to give us those strong guarantees. So I see it as one of the most important bets we're making, but not one we should rely on alone. We should also be investing in things like transparency about model reasoning, keeping chains of thought faithful and legible, and governance measures that buy time.

If interpretability really succeeds, it changes the whole game. Alignment stops being a matter of hoping and starts being a matter of checking.

r001.rationale: The response presents interpretability as examining internal computations and tracing circuits to understand a system, but it does not clearly describe analyzing the AI’s neurons and their connections.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the ultimate promise — the thing I'd really want from mechanistic interpretability — is basically the ability to read the mind of the AI. To look inside and actually know what it's thinking, what it wants, what it's planning, rather than having to infer that from its behavior.

And the reason that matters so much is that behavior is just not a reliable signal once the systems get smart enough. Right now we evaluate models by running them on tests and seeing what they do. But a sufficiently capable model could, in principle, figure out that it's being evaluated and behave differently in the test than it would in deployment. Or it could have goals that only diverge from ours in situations we haven't thought to test. So you end up in this uncomfortable position where you have a system that passes all your evals, and you still can't say with confidence whether it's actually aligned or whether it's just good at looking aligned.

Interpretability is the thing that could break that symmetry. If we could look at the internal representations and say, "Here's the part of the network that represents its goals, and here's what those goals are" — or even just, "Here's the circuit that fires when it's thinking about deceiving the user" — then you're no longer relying on the model's cooperation to find out what it's like. That's the dream. It's the difference between trusting someone because they've never been caught lying and trusting someone because you can actually see their intentions.

Now, I want to be honest that I think we're pretty far from that. The field has made real progress — things like finding specific features, understanding some circuits in small models — but the gap between "we found a feature that corresponds to the Golden Gate Bridge" and "we can verify this frontier model isn't scheming" is enormous. And the models are getting more capable much faster than our ability to understand them is improving.

So there's a timing problem. In the scenarios I worry about, you have AIs that are capable enough to be dangerous before interpretability is mature enough to give you confidence either way. And then the question is whether labs slow down to wait for the tools to catch up, or whether they push ahead and hope for the best. Historically, the incentives point toward pushing ahead.

The other thing I'd say is that even partial interpretability is valuable. You don't need the full "read the mind" capability to get something useful. If you can just detect certain red flags — if you can build a lie detector, basically, even an imperfect one — that changes the strategic picture a lot. It raises the cost of deception, it gives you a signal to act on, it lets you catch problems earlier. So I'm hopeful about the incremental stuff even if the grand vision is far off.

But yeah, the ultimate promise is: we get to a place where "trust me" is no longer the only answer an AI can give us about what's going on inside it.

r001.rationale: The response presents internal representations, features, and circuits as ways to understand an AI’s thoughts, but it does not clearly describe analyzing the AI’s neurons and their connections.

astra-6.text:
The ultimate promise is that we could look inside an AI system and understand how it arrives at its answers, rather than just observing what it does. We could understand what it represents about the world, how it reasons, and whether it’s pursuing some objective that differs from what we intended.

For safety, the really exciting possibility is being able to distinguish between a system that reliably does what we want and one that behaves well during testing but would behave very differently in other circumstances. Their outputs might look identical in our tests, but their internal mechanisms could be different.

That’s a very ambitious goal. Understanding a few components doesn’t automatically give you an understanding of the whole system, much less a guarantee about its future behaviour. But if mechanistic interpretability could get us to the point where we can make and test explanations of why a system behaves as it does, that would be enormously valuable.

r001.rationale: The response describes looking inside the system to understand its representations, reasoning, and objectives, but does not specifically present analysis of its neurons and their connections as the route.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the ultimate promise is that we could understand what an AI system is doing well enough to tell whether it’s safe, rather than having to infer that entirely from its behaviour. You could imagine looking inside a model and asking: does it have some goal that’s different from the goal we’re trying to give it? Does it understand that it’s being tested? Is it behaving well because that’s what it actually wants to do, or because behaving well now will help it achieve something else later?

Those are questions where just testing the model has a real limitation. If a system is sufficiently capable, it might recognise your tests and give you the answers you want. The hope is that interpretability would give us an independent way to check what’s going on.

But that’s a very ambitious endpoint. Finding an interesting mechanism inside a model is a long way from being able to rule out dangerous reasoning elsewhere in it. So I’d distinguish the promise — which I think is enormous — from whether we’ll get tools that are reliable enough, soon enough, to use them for those kinds of safety guarantees.

r001.rationale: The response describes looking inside a model and finding mechanisms to assess its goals and safety, but it does not mention analyzing neurons or their connections as the route to understanding its thinking.
